answer.headline: SFO utilization is high among large hubs, and unmet demand is unmeasured
answer.body:
San Francisco International (SFO) has no catalog metric for unmet demand. What the data provide are calculated utilization measures over {F1.period}: seat factor of {F1}, and the share of departing passengers who flew on capacity-tight route-months.

Seat factor on international=False segments is {F155}. Seat factor on international=True segments is {F156}. The difference is {F308}.

The tight-capacity passenger share is {F2} ({F2.definition}), {F3} ({F3.definition}), and {F4} ({F4.definition}). The difference between the default and middle shares is {F312}. The difference between the middle and highest shares is {F313}. The difference between the default and highest shares is {F314}. The highest share divided by the default share is {F315}.

Among FAA large hubs in the same window, seat-factor P50 is {F47}, P75 is {F48}, and P90 is {F49}. SFO minus those benchmarks is {F289}, {F290}, and {F291}. P90 minus P10 is {F292}. The robust z of SFO seat factor in that set is {F226}.

For the default tight-capacity share, large-hub P50 is {F82}, P75 is {F83}, and P90 is {F84}. SFO minus those benchmarks is {F293}, {F294}, and {F295}. The robust z is {F286}. At the middle threshold, SFO minus P50 is {F296}, minus P75 is {F297}, and minus P90 is {F298} (level {F3}, P50 {F117}, P90 {F119}). At the highest threshold, SFO minus P50 is {F299}, minus P75 is {F300}, and minus P90 is {F301} (level {F4}, P50 {F152}, P90 {F154}).

Versus the prior trailing twelve months ({F5.period}), seat factor changed by {F302} from {F5}, the default tight share changed by {F303} from {F6}, the middle-threshold share changed by {F304} from {F7}, and the highest-threshold share changed by {F305} from {F8}. From CY 2024 to CY 2025, seat factor changed by {F306} (CY 2025 {F9}, CY 2024 {F10}) and the default tight share changed by {F307} (CY 2025 {F11}, CY 2024 {F12}).

Inside {F1.period}, monthly seat factor runs from {F162} ({F162.label}) to {F167} ({F167.label}). That gap is {F309}, which is {F310} times the SFO-minus-median seat-factor gap and {F311} times the large-hub P90-minus-P10 spread.

claims.text: Over {F1.period}, SFO seat factor is {F1} ({F1.class}). international=False seat factor is {F155} and international=True seat factor is {F156}. The difference is {F308}.
Over the same window, the tight-capacity passenger share is {F2} ({F2.definition}), {F3} ({F3.definition}), and {F4} ({F4.definition}).

The difference of the default and middle tight shares is {F312}. The difference of the middle and highest shares is {F313}. The difference of the default and highest shares is {F314}. The highest share divided by the default share is {F315}.
In the large-hub set, seat-factor P50 is {F47}, P75 is {F48}, P90 is {F49}, and P90 minus P10 is {F292}. SFO minus P50 is {F289}, minus P75 is {F290}, and minus P90 is {F291}. The robust z is {F226}.
For the default tight-capacity share, large-hub P50 is {F82}, P75 is {F83}, and P90 is {F84}. SFO minus those benchmarks is {F293}, {F294}, and {F295}. The robust z is {F286}.

At the middle threshold, SFO minus large-hub P50 is {F296}, minus P75 is {F297}, and minus P90 is {F298}. At the highest threshold, SFO minus P50 is {F299}, minus P75 is {F300}, and minus P90 is {F301}.

From {F5.period} to {F1.period}, seat factor changed by {F302}, the default tight share by {F303}, the middle-threshold share by {F304}, and the highest-threshold share by {F305}. From CY 2024 to CY 2025, seat factor changed by {F306} and the default tight share by {F307}.

Monthly seat factor in {F1.period} runs from {F162} ({F162.label}) to {F167} ({F167.label}). The gap is {F309}, equal to {F310} times the SFO-minus-median seat-factor gap and {F311} times the large-hub P90-minus-P10 seat-factor spread.

SFO is in the upper part of the large-hub distribution. Seat factor is {F289} above the median and {F291} versus the P90, inside a P10-to-P90 band of {F292}, with robust z {F226}. The default tight share is {F293} above its median and {F294} above its P75, and {F295} versus its P90, with robust z {F286}. The middle and highest thresholds are above their medians by {F296} and {F299} and differ from their P90s by {F298} and {F301}. The catalog caveat on these metrics is that seat factor varies little across large airports and is not, by itself, evidence of unmet demand.

A route-month that meets a higher seat-factor threshold also meets each lower threshold, and the shares use the same passenger total. {F312} is the passenger share between the default and middle thresholds, {F313} is the share between the middle and highest thresholds, and {F4} is the share at or above the highest threshold. The highest-threshold share is {F315} of the default tight share, so passengers on capacity-tight route-months are concentrated below the highest threshold.

The matched twelve-month changes are {F302} for seat factor and {F303} for the default tight share, with stricter-threshold changes of {F304} and {F305}. CY 2025 is lower than CY 2024 by {F306} on seat factor and by {F307} on the default tight share. These windows do not show utilization tightening into the latest period.

The within-year seat-factor gap of {F309} is {F310} times the gap between SFO and the large-hub median and {F311} times the large-hub P10-to-P90 spread. The annual figure averages a softer month and a fuller month. That range is seasonality in loads on flights that operated.

Fuller flights are consistent with capacity pressure on some route-months, and also with airlines choosing gauge and frequency. These findings do not identify passengers who wanted to fly and did not, a binding terminal or airfield, or a profitable capacity project. Unmet demand stays a hypothesis.

assumptions: SFO is San Francisco International Airport, the unique airport match for that name and code. The San Francisco-Oakland-Fremont CBSA group is a different entity and is not the subject.
Peer percentiles and robust z use FAA large hubs (hub class L), including SFO, over {F1.period}. The percentiles describe that set.
international=False is treated as domestic segments and international=True as international segments.
The three tight-capacity results use the catalog thresholds named in {F2.definition}, {F3.definition}, and {F4.definition}.
Trailing-twelve-month change compares {F1.period} with {F5.period}. Calendar change compares CY 2025 with CY 2024.
Robust z is a descriptive cross-section statistic. The run returned a z for every large hub so the values could be read. It is not a statement that an anomaly screen flagged SFO.
limitations: Unmet demand, terminal capacity, airfield acceptance rates, fares, denied boardings, and profitability are unmeasured. The catalog has no spill metric.
Seat factor varies little across large airports and is not, by itself, evidence of unmet demand. The same caveat is attached to tight-capacity passenger share.
Tight-capacity passenger share counts passengers who departed on route-months above a seat-factor threshold. Demand that never became a booked or scheduled seat is outside the measure.
Seat factor is passengers divided by seats on departing T-100 passenger and combi segments. It is a segment ratio, not an origin-and-destination load factor.
The tight-capacity metric accepts only an airport total, so the domestic, international, and monthly views are for seat factor only.
The robust-z findings carry a generic operator note about outliers. The values to read are {F226} and {F286}.
Monthly seat factor is seasonal. The gap {F309} is a within-year range.
The latest complete calendar comparison is CY 2024 versus CY 2025. The trailing window {F1.period} is the latest level. A full CY 2026 seat factor is not in this extract.
This is not an investment screen and not a valuation.
